claim: AWS supports nine types of policies: identity-based policies, resource-based policies, VPC endpoint policies, permissions boundaries, Organizations SCPs, Organizations RCPs, ACLs, RAM resource shares and session policies.
question: Which policy types does AWS evaluate, according to the IAM policy types page?

values.display: nine types of policies
identity-based policies, resource-based policies, VPC endpoint policies, permissions boundaries

evidence.quote: AWS supports nine types of policies: identity-based policies, resource-based policies, VPC endpoint policies, permissions boundaries, AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs), AWS Organizations resource control policies (RCPs), access control lists (ACLs), Resource Access Manager shares (RAM) and session policies.

claim: A permissions boundary is a managed policy that sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to a user or role; it does not grant permissions on its own, and the entity can perform only the actions allowed by both its identity-based policies and its boundary. A boundary does not limit what a resource-based policy can grant.
question: What does a permissions boundary do, and can it grant permissions?

values.display: does not grant permissions
maximum permissions that an identity-based policy can grant
allowed by both its identity-based policies and its permissions boundaries
do not define the maximum permissions that a resource-based policy can grant

evidence.quote: A permissions boundary is an advanced feature for using a managed policy to set the maximum permissions that an identity-based policy can grant to an IAM entity. An entity's permissions boundary allows it to perform only the actions that are allowed by both its identity-based policies and its permissions boundaries.

That policy defines the maximum permissions that the identity-based policies can grant to an entity, but does not grant permissions. Permissions boundaries do not define the maximum permissions that a resource-based policy can grant to an entity.

claim: An SCP defines the maximum permissions for IAM users and roles in the accounts of an organization or OU; it limits what identity-based and resource-based policies grant, including to each member account root user, and it does not grant permissions.
question: What does a service control policy limit, and can it grant permissions?

values.display: SCPs do not grant permissions
maximum permissions for IAM users and IAM roles
including each AWS account root user

evidence.quote: SCPs limit permissions that identity-based policies or resource-based policies grant to IAM users or IAM roles within the account. SCPs do not grant permissions.

SCPs are JSON policies that specify the maximum permissions for IAM users and IAM roles within accounts of an organization or organizational unit (OU). The SCP limits permissions for principals in member accounts, including each AWS account root user.
SCPs do not grant permissions to the IAM users and IAM roles in your organization. No permissions are granted by an SCP.

claim: SCPs affect only member accounts; they have no effect on users or roles in the management account, and they do not affect service-linked roles.
question: Which accounts and roles are outside the reach of an SCP?

values.display: affect only member accounts
no effect on users or roles in the management account
do not affect any service-linked role

evidence.quote: SCPs affect only member accounts in the organization. They have no effect on users or roles in the management account.
SCPs do not affect any service-linked role. Service-linked roles enable other AWS services to integrate with AWS Organizations and can't be restricted by SCPs.

claim: A session policy is passed when a role or federated user session is created; it limits the permissions that the identity-based policies grant to that session and does not grant permissions.
question: What does a session policy do when you assume a role?

values.display: limit the permissions that the role or user's identity-based policies grant to the session
do not grant permissions

qualifiers.scope: per role or federated user session

evidence.quote: Session policies limit the permissions that the role or user's identity-based policies grant to the session. Session policies limit permissions for a created session, but do not grant permissions.

claim: If any policy type explicitly denies an operation, the request is denied; a Deny statement always prevails over an Allow and can be placed in identity-based, resource-based and service control policies.
question: What happens when one policy allows an action and another policy explicitly denies it?

values.display: explicitly denies access for an operation, then the request is denied
always prevails over an Allow statement
any type of policy, including identity-based, resource-based, and service control policies

evidence.quote: If any one of these policy types explicitly denies access for an operation, then the request is denied.

If a Deny statement applies to an access request, it always prevails over an Allow statement. For example, if you allow access to all actions in AWS but deny access to IAM, any request to IAM is denied. You can include a Deny statement in any type of policy, including identity-based, resource-based, and service control policies with AWS Organizations.

claim: When a request is affected by an SCP, a permissions boundary and an identity-based policy, it is allowed only if all three allow it; the effective permissions are the intersection of the three.
question: How do an SCP, a permissions boundary and an identity-based policy combine for one request?

values.display: allowed only if all three policy types allow it
intersection of all three policy types

evidence.quote: An IAM entity (user or role) can make a request that is affected by an SCP, a permissions boundary, and an identity-based policy. In this case, the request is allowed only if all three policy types allow it. The effective permissions are the intersection of all three policy types.
If both a permissions boundary (an advanced IAM feature) and an SCP are present, then the boundary, the SCP, and the identity-based policy must all allow the action.

claim: A resource-based policy grants permissions to the principal named in the policy, and that principal can be in the same account as the resource or in another account.
question: Who receives the permissions in a resource-based policy?

values.display: grant permissions to the principal that is specified in the policy
same account as the resource or in other accounts

evidence.quote: Resource-based policies grant permissions to the principal that is specified in the policy. Principals can be in the same account as the resource or in other accounts.

claim: For a request from one account to a resource in another, the requester needs an identity-based policy in its own account that allows the request and the resource-based policy in the resource account must allow the requester; without both the request fails. Within one account a resource-based policy alone is enough.
question: Which policies are needed for cross-account access to a resource that has a resource-based policy?

values.display: policies in both accounts that allow the operation
otherwise the request fails
no additional identity-based policy is required

qualifiers.condition: the principal and the resource are in separate AWS accounts

evidence.quote: For requests made from one account to another, the requester in Account A must have an identity-based policy that allows them to make a request to the resource in Account B. Also, the resource-based policy in Account B must allow the requester in Account A to access the resource. There must be policies in both accounts that allow the operation, otherwise the request fails.

When the principal and the resource are in separate AWS accounts, you must also use an identity-based policy to grant the principal access to the resource. However, if a resource-based policy grants access to a principal in the same account, no additional identity-based policy is required.

claim: The only resource-based policy in IAM is the role trust policy; a role is both an identity and a resource, so it needs both a trust policy (who can assume it) and an identity-based permissions policy (what it can do).
question: What is a role trust policy, and why does a role need two policies?

values.display: only one type of resource-based policy called a role trust policy
attach both a trust policy and an identity-based policy to an IAM role
define which principal entities (accounts, users, roles, and federated users) can assume the role

evidence.quote: The IAM service supports only one type of resource-based policy called a role trust policy, which is attached to an IAM role. An IAM role is both an identity and a resource that supports resource-based policies. For that reason, you must attach both a trust policy and an identity-based policy to an IAM role. Trust policies define which principal entities (accounts, users, roles, and federated users) can assume the role.

claim: Resource-based policies, for example on S3 buckets, SQS queues, VPC endpoints and KMS keys, define who can access a resource and are the way to grant direct cross-account access without a role.
question: When does the FAQ say to use a resource-based policy?

values.display: grant direct, cross-account access
Amazon S3 buckets, Amazon SQS queues, VPC endpoints, and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption keys

evidence.quote: With resource-based policies, you can define who has access to a resource and which actions they can perform with it. For example, you can attach resource-based policies to Amazon S3 buckets, Amazon SQS queues, VPC endpoints, and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption keys. Use resource-based policies to grant direct, cross-account access.

claim: Resource-based policies are inline only; there are no managed resource-based policies.
question: Can a resource-based policy be a managed policy?

values.display: inline only, not managed
no managed resource-based policies

evidence.quote: Resource-based policies are inline only, not managed.
Resource-based policies are inline policies. There are no managed resource-based policies.

claim: Permissions of a user and of an assumed role are not cumulative: only one set is active at a time, the user gives up their own permissions while in the role, and gets them back on exit.
question: Does a user keep their own permissions while using an assumed role?

values.display: not cumulative
Only one set of permissions is active at a time
automatically restored

evidence.quote: The permissions of your IAM user and any roles that you assume are not cumulative. Only one set of permissions is active at a time. When you assume a role, you temporarily give up your previous user or role permissions and work with the permissions that are assigned to the role. When you exit the role, your user permissions are automatically restored.

While using the role, the user can perform only the actions and access only the resources permitted by the role; their original user permissions are suspended. When the user exits the role, the original user permissions are restored.

claim: An IAM role gives access through temporary security credentials; it has a set of permissions but is not associated with a specific user or group, and trusted entities such as identity providers or AWS services assume it. AWS calls relying on short-term credentials a security best practice.
question: What is an IAM role, and why does AWS recommend roles?

values.display: relying on temporary security credentials
not associated with a specific user or group
relying on short-term credentials, a security best practice

evidence.quote: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles provide a way to access AWS by relying on temporary security credentials. Each role has a set of permissions for making AWS service requests, and a role is not associated with a specific user or group. Instead, trusted entities such as identity providers or AWS services assume roles.
Use IAM roles to grant access to your AWS accounts by relying on short-term credentials, a security best practice.

claim: An IAM user has long-term credentials (a password and access keys); a role has no standard long-term credentials and gives temporary security credentials for each role session. AWS recommends relying on temporary credentials instead of creating IAM users where possible.
question: What is the credential difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

values.display: does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys
IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys
identities with long-term credentials

evidence.quote: Also, a role does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys, associated with it. Instead, when you assume a role, it provides you with temporary security credentials for your role session. Unlike IAM roles, IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys. Where possible, best practices recommend relying on temporary credentials instead of creating IAM users who have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys.
IAM users are identities with long-term credentials.

claim: Long-term access keys of IAM users and the root user stay valid until you revoke them by hand; temporary credentials from roles and STS expire after a short period, which limits the damage of an accidental exposure.
question: Why are temporary credentials safer than long-term access keys?

values.display: remain valid until you manually revoke them
expire after a short period of time
reduce your risk in case credentials are accidentally exposed

evidence.quote: Long-term access keys, such as those associated with IAM users and the root user, remain valid until you manually revoke them. However, temporary security credentials obtained through IAM roles and other features of the AWS Security Token Service expire after a short period of time. Use temporary security credentials to help reduce your risk in case credentials are accidentally exposed.

claim: Temporary security credentials have a limited lifetime that you can set up to a maximum, and after they expire they cannot be reused; you do not have to rotate or revoke them.
question: What happens to temporary security credentials after they expire?

values.display: cannot be reused
limited lifetime
up to a maximum limit

evidence.quote: The temporary security credentials have a limited lifetime, so you do not have to update them or explicitly revoke them when they're no longer needed. After temporary security credentials expire, they cannot be reused. You can specify how long the credentials are valid, up to a maximum limit.
After the credentials expire, AWS no longer recognizes them or allows any kind of access from API requests made with them.

claim: On an AWS compute service such as EC2 or Lambda, AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to the compute resource; SDK applications find and use them, so there is no need to distribute long-lived IAM user credentials to workloads on AWS.
question: How does an application on EC2 or Lambda get credentials without access keys?

values.display: AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource
no need to distribute long lived credentials for an IAM user

evidence.quote: When you're building on an AWS compute service, such as Amazon EC2 or Lambda, AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource. Applications written using an AWS SDK will discover and use these temporary credentials to access AWS resources, and there is no need to distribute long lived credentials for an IAM user to your workloads running on AWS.

claim: IAM best practice: human users use temporary credentials by federating through an identity provider and assuming roles; for centralized access management AWS recommends IAM Identity Center.
question: How does AWS recommend that human users access AWS?

values.display: Require your human users to use temporary credentials
we recommend that you use AWS IAM Identity Center

evidence.quote: Require your human users to use temporary credentials when accessing AWS. You can use an identity provider for your human users to provide federated access to AWS accounts by assuming roles, which provide temporary credentials. For centralized access management, we recommend that you use AWS IAM Identity Center (IAM Identity Center) to manage access to your accounts and permissions within those accounts.
You might be using IAM users for workforce users. In this case, AWS recommends using an identity provider and federating into AWS by assuming roles.

claim: Long-term IAM user access keys remain the answer only for workloads that cannot use roles (for example WordPress plugins) and for third-party clients or vendors not hosted on AWS that do not support Identity Center.
question: When does AWS still accept IAM user access keys instead of roles?

values.display: you can't use IAM roles to provide temporary credentials, such as for WordPress plugins
third-party AWS clients or vendors that are not hosted on AWS

qualifiers.condition: scenarios in which you need IAM users with programmatic access

evidence.quote: In some situations, you can't use IAM roles to provide temporary credentials, such as for WordPress plugins. In these situations, use IAM user long-term access keys for that workload to authenticate to AWS.
If you are using tools that don’t support access with IAM Identity Center, such as third-party AWS clients or vendors that are not hosted on AWS, use IAM user long-term access keys.
